newsitem.title: UK: U.S. Treasuries rise in London, long end popular.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries rise in London, long end popular.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries firmed up in London trade on Friday, extending a positive streak begun after a batch of data on Thursday showing slower U.S. economic activity, dealers and analysts said.
Traders said 10-year notes and 30-year bonds were bid but they added that the market was unlikely to see dramatic action, with only trade figures due at 1230 GMT to attract any interest.

"We've seen a little better buying in 10s and bonds," said a dealer at a U.S. bank in London. He said a $750 million Eurobond launched on Friday was proving successful and was helping the tone. On top of that, the technical picture had brightened.
"We got through the 110-27 yesterday -- that was a key level," the trader said.

The U.S. long bond at 1000 GMT was at 99-18, yielding 6.78 percent, compared with 99-12/15 at the Tokyo finish and 99-11/12 at the New York close. The December T-bond in automated trade was at 111-13, up from 111-04 at Chicago's Thursday settlement.

Suedwestdeutsche LB Capital Markets Plc earlier launched a $750 million five-year bond at 14 basis points over Treasuries. The U.S. bank trader said that had been increased from an originally planned $500 million.
Tom Rayner, economist at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull in London, said figures on Thursday reaffirmed a belief that the Federal Reserve can hold off tightening monetary policy until 1997.

Data on industrial production, capacity utilisation, housing starts, and the Philadelphia Fed index all were released on Thursday and the overall picture was of a slowdown in U.S. growth, economists said.
"By maintaining things as they have, the Fed have limited the downside (for Treasuries) so if bonds do soften it's not going to be as aggressive as previously thought," Rayner said.
He said his bank was now looking for long bond yields around seven percent at year-end rather than a previous 7.25 forecast.
U.S. August international trade numbers are due at 1230 GMT, with economists expecting a deficit of $8.5 billion.
